---
name: orchestrated-dev
description: "Orchestrate large multi-slice development across files or sessions, new feature slices and refactors alike: scope slices, dispatch model-matched workers in owned worktrees, review, integrate and maintain a tracked handoff. Use for explicit delegated implementation; ordinary one-session changes use the normal branch/PR workflow."
---

# Orchestrated Dev

Portable Claude Code skill: copy this folder into `<repo>/.claude/skills/` or `~/.claude/skills/`; never over a same-named skill another installer manages. It assumes git and Claude Code; every other tool is detected at run start and used only when present.

The main session only scopes, dispatches, reviews, commits Codex slices, integrates, merges and hands off; workers implement slices. The repo's own CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md rules bind every worker; carry the essentials in its prompt.

`<root>` is the absolute primary checkout; `<run-id>` is `<slug>-<6 random hex>`, recorded once and reused. Manual worktrees: `<root>/.tmp/worktrees/<run-id>-<slice-id>`. `<state>`: `<root>/.tmp/orchestrated-refactor/<run-id>/<slice-id>/`; an isolated worker's state lives inside its worktree at `.tmp/orchestrated-refactor/<run-id>/<slice-id>/`. Record resolved paths. Slice ids are never `review`. Shell commands here are bash; in PowerShell use 7.4+ (older versions re-encode `>` output). If `.tmp/` is not ignored, append `.tmp/` to `$(git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir)/info/exclude` (local, covers every worktree, no commit); operational state is ignored, the run handoff is tracked.

## Qualify

Use only for multi-file or multi-session work (new feature slices or a refactor), or explicit delegated implementation. Work that fits one session uses the normal workflow.

## Phase 0 - Environment detect

Run once per session before any edit; record results in the handoff's Environment table when Phase 1 creates it. Later sections apply an optional tool only when it was detected here.

| Check | Command / marker | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Codex | `codex --version`, `codex login status` | Cross-family review lens and optional workers |
| RTK | `rtk --version`; an `rtk` PreToolUse hook in `~/.claude/settings.json` or `.claude/settings*.json` | Worker TOOLING line |
| Graphify | `graphify-out/graph.json` exists and `graphify` on PATH; may be stale, so confirm graph answers against the code | One scoping query |
| GitHub CLI | `gh auth status` | PR creation, CI status |
| Default branch | `git symbolic-ref --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD` (strip `origin/`); if unset, `gh repo view --json defaultBranchRef -q .defaultBranchRef.name` or `git remote set-head origin --auto` and retry | Worktree base, PR target |
| MCP servers | `claude mcp list` (starts configured servers, including repo-defined ones; run only in a repo you trust) | Tooling line per slice |
| Toolchain | SDK pins, lockfiles, package engines, test runners, Compose files | Slice GATE commands |
| Platform | OS and shell | Worktree serialization, command syntax |

Report required but absent tools with the exact install command and what they unblock. Install nothing and change no global config without the user's yes.

## Phase 1 - Scope (orchestrator)

1. If Graphify was detected, query it once for the affected area; otherwise use targeted search.
2. Design before slicing when the work will take more than one slice and those slices would share a lifecycle or need one shared mechanism, or when it touches money, security, data lifecycle or concurrency; a handed `full-review` plan is exempt (Handed plan, below). Write a tracked design record (repo convention, else `docs/plans/<slug>-design.md`, linked from the handoff; a held fix (the global held-fix rule) keeps the record, lens passes and every other record this step makes in `.tmp/<task>/review/` only, never in a tracked file or the handoff):
   - one state machine or pure decision type per lifecycle, with numbered rules (states, transitions, guards, outcomes);
   - one contract per shared mechanism the work needs: lock order, idempotency-key scheme, outbound-provider-call protocol (such as receipt before call), failure classification and error codes, handler outcome types, sweep runner, notification/alert/audit/timeline path, cache invalidation, access enforcement and the page state and refresh rule (both defined below). Each names its one implementation, its callers and how a new caller joins, and is marked as follows (one mechanism per job).
     - Marks: mark each mechanism a change needs reuse, extend or new, in that order of preference. Reuse where the repo has exactly one implementation for that job and it fits; extend where that one falls short or two or more exist (consolidate them into one, even when one already fits); new only where none exists or extending cannot meet the need.
     - Retirement: a consolidation or replacement records why and names every implementation it retires. The mechanism slice that extends or builds the surviving one, with any slices a split move continues in, moves every caller to it; the last of them deletes the retired ones, except a reader that persisted or in-flight data still needs, kept with its removal condition (global Data rule).
     - Access enforcement: authorization is one decision point, computed once per resource acted on (per request, or per item where a request or job acts on several) from its principal, action and resource, that every handler, background caller and UI asks. A lower layer enforcing the decision it is handed is not a second check, but recomputing it or applying divergent rules is. A job acting for a user (a message handler, sweep or bulk processor running as the stored caller) takes that user's decision, per item. A platform job, which runs with no requesting user, transitions the facts the decision reads (standing, lifecycle or policy, such as a billing sweep that suspends an account, or a data-exit sweep that moves a suspended one to terminated; its export or deletion of data is not a transition). Those transitions, and the reads their guards need, run through the lifecycle type that governs them and are not callers of the access decision; a request that triggers one takes its principal's decision first. The design record names each such transition with its lifecycle type and guard reads; the access decision stays the only reader of those facts for access. Any other read, write, export or delete of users' resources by a system job, in the same job or another, goes through the same decision point as a named service principal.
     - Page state and refresh rule: a UI defines once what a route or query change re-initializes and what it keeps, and a data component's refresh re-renders that component and what depends on its data, never remounting or resetting unrelated page state.
     - Reach: set queries over growing tables (tables written per user action, event, message or job run) share one reach definition per resource and scope. The record names its branches, the index that drives each and, where it has several branches, the union-of-id-sets form: each branch its own index-driven query, then select by id.

   Design lens: a fresh-context reviewer (Review path opus Claude reviewer form, else the Codex form; never the authoring conversation; with neither, it goes to the user like an open finding) reads the goal, the record and the code it touches.
   - It reports:
     - missing lifecycles or mechanisms;
     - a rule or mechanism defined twice;
     - a contract whose mark is missing or wrong against the marks defined above and the repo's existing mechanisms;
     - a retirement whose recorded reason does not hold or that misses an existing implementation or caller;
     - contracts that conflict or that a slice would have to bypass;
     - a contract a slice cannot follow as written (its literal reading is impossible or contradictory).
   - Each finding names the contracts and slices it touches, including a slice that needs a mechanism the record lacks.
   - Severity: HIGH is any of those defects; MEDIUM is a contract with more than one valid reading for a realistic case a slice will meet; LOW is wording.
   - Fix or rebut each finding; a LOW never holds dispatch. A changed contract gets one more lens pass, except an open item's resolution within its slice's contracts, which that slice's review covers (Convergence); one that changes another slice's contract stops with "needs contract". A slice group gets at most two passes before its open HIGH and MEDIUM findings, new or earlier, go to the user (Convergence).
   - Per-slice gating: a slice dispatches once a pass run after the last change to each contract and decision type it needs (those on its CONTRACTS line and any mechanism a finding says it lacks) covered them, and no open HIGH or MEDIUM touches them other than one Convergence lets through. Slices an open finding does not touch proceed.
   - Scoped passes: a later pass may cover only the contracts of the slices to dispatch next. It reads the goal, the record and the code those contracts touch, plus the previous pass's report and the record diff since it. It states fixed, partially fixed or not fixed for each earlier finding and reports only new defects.
   - Convergence: a pass with no HIGH or MEDIUM is sound for the slices it covered. A finding still open after the extra pass, or after a group's second pass, goes to the user before dispatching a slice it touches (an unattended run applies its caller's needs-human signal and holds those slices).
     - The user's decision to continue is recorded. At most one further pass then runs for the slices that finding touches (its slice group), never one per later decision.
     - After it, an open MEDIUM, or a HIGH that only makes a contract unfollowable as written (not a missing or second mechanism, or a rule decided twice), becomes an open item on the CONTRACTS line of the one undispatched slice that carries that contract, and that slice dispatches.
     - Any other open HIGH, and an open finding on a contract that several slices or a dispatched slice carry, goes back to the user with no further pass. The user drops or redesigns the slices it touches, or lets them dispatch with the finding recorded. A redesign starts a fresh round: one pass on its changed contracts, then Convergence again.
     - The worker resolves an open item within its contracts and reports the resolution, or stops with "needs contract". The slice's own review covers the resolution (Feedback loop).
   - Record each pass in the handoff: scope, lens, model, verdict and HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW counts.

   Run in flight (outside a handed `full-review` plan):
   - Trigger, for a run this step covers:
     - it resumes, or adopts these rules mid-run, without a design record that holds every lifecycle the work has and contracts every mechanism the list above names that the work uses; or
     - it takes a redesign (Review path), whose lifecycles and mechanisms count toward this step's condition.
   - Before dispatching any further slice, write or update the record: the lifecycles and contracts for what remains, each mechanism already merged marked as the contract bullet above says.
   - Then run the design lens, after (not instead of) any redesign lens.
   - Remaining worker prompts carry the CONTRACTS line. Slices already dispatched get it by message (Feedback loop) and are checked against the record before they integrate.
   - A conflicting slice never integrates a second implementation. The design lens picks, once per mechanism, the one that survives. With no lens, or a pick it cannot make, the user picks before that slice integrates (an unattended run applies its caller's needs-human signal and stops).
     - The record's survives: the slice is reworked onto it on its own branch.
     - The slice's survives: its mechanism part moves into a mechanism slice under Phase 1 step 3, marked extend or new, whose contract enters the record with one more lens pass before it dispatches. It is ordered before every slice that uses it, carries its architecture tests and moves the other callers; the feature remainder depends on it.
   - A parallel implementation already merged is an existing mechanism, marked like any other.
   - A run already integrated on one branch that cannot meet ship in increments (Integrate and merge) records that exception in the handoff. Its PR is reviewed under the Large PR rule (Review path), which applies by size.

   Handed plan (a `full-review` plan handed to this run):
   - Its slices, order, approval marks and shared-mechanism contracts are taken as written, never redesigned here. Each row records its reviewed SHA, evidence paths and, once merged, its commit SHAs (step 5).
   - Freshness: at adoption, before each slice dispatches and again before it merges, after a fetch, `git log --oneline <reviewed-sha>..origin/<default> -- <SCOPE and evidence paths>` must be empty, ignoring the `full-review` report and its amendment commits, this run's handoff commits and the commits of the plan's merged slices ordered before it.
   - Otherwise stop all further plan dispatch. Queued slices stay queued and the stop is the recorded next action; in-flight slices finish, each checked before merge and stopped if stale itself.
   - Give the stopped slice to the user, who drops it (every live slice ordered after it then goes to the user too), accepts it unchanged (its row records the current default head as reviewed SHA) or starts a `full-review` re-run whose plan replaces every live unmerged row. Dispatch resumes only when no slice awaits that choice and no re-run is pending.
   - A dropped row stays in the table as `dropped by the user`, a replaced one as superseded. A stopped, dropped or replaced row keeps its branch, PR and worktree until the user decides about them.
   - An approval-marked slice, and one accepted unchanged, dispatches only after the user's yes.
3. Slice by explicit paths, spec and runnable finish line, leaving context reserve for tool output and edits. Each slice owns a branch; serialize dependencies and parallelize independent work. Split anything that needs the reserve to fit.
   - Slice by mechanism as well as feature. When the design record names a shared mechanism, slice 0:
     - extends the mechanisms marked extend and builds those marked new, never a second implementation beside one the repo keeps;
     - adds one end-to-end path through every mechanism the record names;
     - adds architecture tests (the repo's existing tool, else plain tests in its framework) asserting one implementation per mechanism, reused ones included, and one caller per wrapped gateway or IO entry point. A kept reader the design record lists with its removal condition is excluded until that condition is met.
   - When slice 0, or a caller move, exceeds one slice's reserve, split it into mechanism slices in dependency order, all ordered before the slices that use them:
     - the first also adds the tests the repo lacks for reused mechanisms;
     - each one's architecture tests cover the mechanisms built, extended or reused so far;
     - a caller move may continue in the next. Each slice of it leaves both implementations working, and the one-implementation assertion for that mechanism lands in the slice that completes the move and retirement. A mid-move slice that stops or is dropped goes to the user with the two-implementation state named;
     - the last adds the end-to-end path.
   - When every contract is marked reuse, slice 0 only adds what the repo lacks of those architecture tests and of a passing end-to-end path through the mechanisms. There is no slice 0 when it lacks neither.
   - A mechanism added later (Feedback loop) gets its own mechanism slice when it needs one, held to the same tests, which moves any caller of a parallel path to it.
   - Feature slices depend on the mechanism slices they use and own no mechanism. Plan the PRs per Integrate and merge (ship in increments).
4. At open behavior choices, prefer entity/target-scoped configuration or data policy when it needs no significant redesign; record the policy shape in SCOPE. Where an `engineering-criteria` skill or copy is available, each slice's CRITERIA line attaches the files its Packs table selects for what the slice touches, by file and never retyped, and a slice that adds or changes a set query over a growing table names each query's driving index and plan check in DONE. Without an `engineering-criteria` skill or copy, each slice builds the right design even when it costs more than a narrow patch: it removes the duplication it touches (reuse or extract a shared helper), keeps one decision point per rule (for example one state machine instead of status checks spread across handlers) and keeps one mechanism per job, searching the repo first and reusing or extending its existing one before building one (for example one idempotency-key builder every handler uses instead of each formatting its own), without over-engineering. Its queries over a table that grows with use cost in proportion to the rows their driving index selects, never to the table: an index drives each filter, join key and paged ordering, with no OR across correlated subqueries, and no function on the filtered column or leading-wildcard search unless an index built for that expression or search serves it, and a new or changed set query gets a plan check, taken under conditions that keep the planner's choice stable whatever the row counts, asserting each read of such a table goes through the driving index named for it and is bounded by that index's condition, or by the limit where the index supplies the order with no filter or sort between, on every supported provider. When a second fix for the same failure or flow fails, or a fix surfaces a new failure there, the slice stops patching and changes the approach at the shared cause, within the slice's SCOPE; a change beyond it is reported as a blocker naming what and why, which the orchestrator re-scopes or takes to the user (a handed `full-review` plan is never re-planned here). Either way, each slice carries the design record's contracts and decision types it uses into SCOPE.
5. Create the tracked handoff, or continue the one the run already has (repo convention, else `docs/plans/<slug>-handoff.md`): run id, goal, design record link and design lens passes (step 2; a held fix records neither here), decisions, Environment table, next action, active count, FIFO queue and slice table. Each row records scope, weight, family/model/substitutions, status, branch/PR, worktree, worker/thread id and state path, plus, for a handed `full-review` slice, its reviewed SHA, evidence paths and, once merged, its commit SHAs.

## Model assignment

Routing as of 2026-10; re-check vendor docs and coding benchmarks when a new model ships. Missing evidence is not endorsement.

| Model | Route here | Never route here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| haiku | Extraction, inventory/verification sweeps and doc-only work with explicit paths and cheaply checked results | Coding or large-input recall |
| sonnet | Clear-spec implementation, mechanical multi-file changes, tests with a runnable check; precision-first review | Unmeasured recall-first, long-horizon or toolchain work |
| opus | Hard cross-file/architecture/long-horizon coding; build/dependency/toolchain work; recall-first review | - |
| fable | Reasoning escalation after opus fails; security review | Build, dependency, packaging, toolchain; exploits or attack tooling |
| codex (if detected) | Fat independent coding/test slices with paths, spec and runnable check; cross-family review | Small/correction-heavy slices, or context that cannot be carried in the prompt |
| main session | Scope, dispatch, review, Codex slice commits, integration, merge, handoff | Slice implementation |

Pass family aliases (`haiku`, `sonnet`, `opus`, `fable`), never dated model ids or model-default env overrides. Record the model that actually served each slice. Review never uses a model banned for the subject.

Availability fallback: fable -> opus; opus -> sonnet with a smaller scope; haiku -> sonnet; sonnet -> opus. Record substitutions. Never cross a subject ban; if none is eligible, ask.

## Recommended settings

| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Orchestrator | opus, `/effort high`; consider a larger autocompact window for long runs and record it in the handoff |
| Workers | Inherit effort unless overridden; use per-call `effort: "high"` when the session runs at xhigh or max and announce it |
| Codex | Newest listed `gpt-<version>-sol` from `codex debug models` (highest version with `visibility: list`) for workers and review, resolved before every worker launch and review lens; a resume keeps its session's model (if no sol model is listed, use the strongest listed non-astra model and record the substitution); explicit `-m` on exec, explicit `-c model_reasoning_effort=<level>` and `-c model_auto_compact_token_limit=230000 -c model_auto_compact_token_limit_scope=total` on every exec/resume (keeps input under the 272K price band). Never `astra` or `ultra` |

## Delegation mechanics

Implementation: `Agent`, `subagent_type: general-purpose`, family `model`, `isolation: "worktree"`, background by default. Search sweeps may use Explore without isolation.

Isolated agents cannot write outside their worktree. When a slice needs that (or the shell hook refuses isolated git), use a non-isolated agent restricted by prompt to a manual worktree. Run `git fetch origin` first, then `git worktree add "<root>/.tmp/worktrees/<run-id>-<slice-id>" -b <type>/<run-id>-<slice-id> origin/<default-branch>`, where `<type>` is `feature`, `fix`, `chore` or `docs`.

On Windows serialize worktree creation, including harness-managed spawns (at most one isolation spawn per message). Before dispatch create manual `<state>` or pass the isolated worker a state path relative to its worktree.

Codex worker (only if detected and logged in): create the manual worktree and `<state>`, resolve the model (Recommended settings), then run in background from bash (every Codex form here reads its prompt from standard input through the `-` argument; PowerShell 7+: `Get-Content -Raw -LiteralPath "<file>" | codex exec ... -`):

`codex exec --json -s workspace-write -m <model> -c model_reasoning_effort=<medium|high> -c model_auto_compact_token_limit=230000 -c model_auto_compact_token_limit_scope=total -C "<worktree>" --add-dir "<state>" --output-last-message "<state>/report.md" - < "<state>/prompt.md" > "<state>/log.jsonl"`

Write each prompt or correction to a file at an absolute path and feed it on standard input, never as a command-line argument or inline text: bash `< "<file>"`, PowerShell 7+ `Get-Content -Raw -LiteralPath "<file>" | <command>` (Windows PowerShell 5.1 re-encodes piped text). Assume a large prompt: it carries criteria files and findings and can pass the operating system's argument limit (about 32,000 characters on Windows). Double-quoted inline text is also expanded by the shell (`$(...)` and backticks in bash, `$var` and `$(...)` in PowerShell), so quoted PR, issue or diff text could run commands. Quote every path.

Effort: medium for clear-spec slices, high for cross-file work. Record the thread id from the first `thread.started` event; never read the full JSONL. Correct from `<worktree>` (resume has no `-C` or `-s`): `codex exec resume --json -c sandbox_mode=workspace-write -c 'sandbox_workspace_write.writable_roots=["<state>"]' -c model_reasoning_effort=<level> -c model_auto_compact_token_limit=230000 -c model_auto_compact_token_limit_scope=total --output-last-message "<state>/report.md" <thread-id> - < "<state>/correction.md" >> "<state>/log.jsonl"`; the session keeps its model. Use forward slashes in `<state>` inside that TOML value. The sandbox cannot write a linked worktree's git metadata, so Codex workers do not commit: their BRANCH line says "leave changes uncommitted", and the orchestrator commits in `<worktree>` after reviewing the diff. The orchestrator commits (`git -C "<worktree>" add -A` after checking `git status` for stray files, then `git commit`) after each reviewed report, before each resume and before abandoning or respawning a stopped worker, so a lost worktree or replacement worker starts from that commit. This overrides any repo rule telling workers to commit. Network is off and writes outside `<worktree>`/`<state>` fail (package caches, SDK first-run state, browser installs): restore/prepare in `<worktree>` before dispatch, or keep such slices on Claude workers. The sandbox still reads anything the user can: trusted slices only.

## Worker prompt template

Adapt this into every prompt, including cold replacement workers:

```
SCOPE: <paths, change, explicit non-goals and chosen policy shape>
DONE: <runnable finish line>
CONTRACTS: <design record path and the contracts and decision types this slice uses, verbatim, or a handed `full-review` plan's shared-mechanism contracts; "none" when neither exists>. Use these and the mechanisms the repo already has; never add a parallel one (another lock, key format, access enforcement point, notification path, cache eviction, page state and refresh rule or outcome type). If the slice needs a shared mechanism, or a rule another slice also decides, that neither provides, stop and report "needs contract: <what, why>"; never invent one. Each open item it lists (design lens Convergence): resolve it within those contracts and report the resolution, or stop with "needs contract". Rules local to this slice need no contract.
CRITERIA: <where an `engineering-criteria` skill or copy is available, the files its Packs table selects for SCOPE, the core file first: appended whole below this prompt, or given as paths to read in full before editing; otherwise "none">; repo facts file <path, or "absent">. They bind this slice; where SCOPE conflicts with one, stop and report.
REUSE: before adding a shared helper, script, engine or mechanism, search this repo and the shared locations the facts file names; reuse, else extend, else new.
TESTS: each test at the lowest level that fails when the behavior breaks (unit, integration against the real dependency through the repo's existing harness, API/contract, architecture; E2E only for primary journeys); no sleeps, real clocks, unrecorded seeds, real external services, shared mutable state or assertions that cannot fail where they would hide or fake a regression; a new test framework, library or fixture only when requested, except a needed accessibility checker or real-dependency integration harness, justified as a dependency per `engineering-criteria` License stability (platform or first-party first, then a permissive or weak-copyleft, community-governed component; a single-vendor one only when none fits, with the reason recorded; a source-available, commercial or already-moved one only with user approval, so report it); a new expensive tier (E2E, load, mutation, suites over about 10 minutes) gets manual-dispatch CI only. Source: `engineering-criteria` Tests. Smoke suites and integration tiers that reach real network or cloud services follow `engineering-criteria` Resilience; unit tests still use no real external services.
Complete the scope, nothing else. Report pre-existing concerns unless required for this change. Resolve ambiguity from wording and surrounding code; state assumptions. Follow repo test patterns; leave a runnable check for each non-trivial branch or parser.
TOOLING: <shell to use; "a hook rewrites commands through rtk, do not hand-prefix" | "no rtk">. Use native tools for files, targeted reads and surgical edits. MCP/CLIs for this slice: <list>.
GATE: narrowest behavior check. Report command/result, failures and anything that cannot run/why; a failed start or syntax-only substitute is not a pass. Report each test tier's duration. Where the slice touches code whose behavior can differ between the repo's supported configurations (those its instructions, settings switches or provider lists declare, such as two database providers or a flag's states), run the changed tests on each configuration, or report "needs orchestrator: <command, configuration>" for one that cannot run here. No extra review/hardening or reviewer subagents; the orchestrator schedules review.
BRANCH: only <worktree>/<branch>. Commit completed items/resumable checkpoints with plain messages; never merge, push to the default branch or touch another checkout.
STATE: <absolute state path, or isolated relative path resolved against worktree root>.
HANDOFF: create <state>/handoff.md before investigation; update after commits/blockers and before reporting: scope, branch/worktree/worker id, commits, decisions, verification, blockers and exact next action.
CODEX ONLY: replace the BRANCH line with "BRANCH: only <worktree>; leave changes uncommitted; the orchestrator commits." and in HANDOFF/REPORT read "commits" as "changed files".
REPORT: at most about 30 lines covering the whole slice: changes/why, files, actual checks, decisions, risks and last commit. Tool-backed claims only; mark unverified. No transcripts/full diffs. Then, outside the 30 lines, each inventory the Packs table lists for the attached files (REUSE, QUERIES, ENTRY POINTS), `none` where empty; with no CRITERIA files, each new shared helper or mechanism with the search that found none.
```

## Feedback loop (orchestrator)

1. Read the completion report and the real diff, not just the self-report. Done means diff reviewed and narrow checks green; update the slice table immediately. Fold every pre-existing concern a worker reports in this repository, related to the task or not, into the run as a slice or queue entry, except outside a scope the user narrowed, in a run adopted from `full-review` (held weaknesses the plan omits may sit near the code), or in another repository: those go to the user in the final report, or through its caller when unattended. An unattended run folds in the rest the same way; a product decision, what its caller's gate would hold the change for, anything outside the PR's own change found during a repair of an open PR, anything found when its own task makes no change, and work too large to review with its change go through its caller, or an issue, with the reason. Doc gaps beyond the changed members and their containing type's own declaration are not folded in unless the user scoped doc work. A security or data-exposure defect goes only to the user (through its caller when unattended), never into a tracked file, commit, PR, issue or comment text, until the user decides how it is fixed. Defer only work too complex for the session, with the reason. A resolved CONTRACTS open item: the slice's review also checks the resolution against the design lens's defects for that contract (its prompt carries the open item, the lens findings on it and the resolution); a HIGH or MEDIUM there is fixed like any review finding, or the slice stops with "needs contract". Record the resolution in the design record before the slice integrates. A "needs contract" report: extend the design record (writing one as Run in flight (Phase 1 step 2) describes if the run has none, whether or not step 2 covered the run; one design lens pass on the change), marking the contract reuse, extend or new as in Phase 1 step 2; a mechanism slice the waiting slices depend on (never reopening a merged mechanism slice) extends or builds it, or for one reused as is adds only what the repo lacks of the architecture tests and of the end-to-end path for it. When a slice runs, bring its commits into each waiting slice's branch (merge default once it merges, keeping the worker's commits and taking the mechanism code from default on conflict) and send the worker the new contract with that commit; with no slice (a reused mechanism that lacks neither), first bring default into each waiting slice's branch that lacks that mechanism or its tests (same merge rule), then send the worker the contract, with that commit when one was made. In a run executing a handed `full-review` plan, the slice stops and goes to the user instead of re-planning; slices that depend on it stay queued.
2. Send corrections to the same worker (SendMessage, or Codex resume) with a phase excerpt, handoff and diff. First confirm its worktree still exists; never resume into a removed worktree, since the worker may fall back into the primary checkout. Respawn only if unreachable or the worktree is gone.
3. Usage-limit or auth errors are not failures to retry: queue the slice for that family's reset or route it to another eligible family, and record it. Mechanical failure: one same-config retry with the primary error. Reasoning failure: re-dispatch one tier up (haiku -> sonnet -> opus -> fable unless banned; Codex medium -> high, then stop). At the top eligible model, stop with evidence. At most two escalations.
4. Open items without a blocker get a concrete continue, not a respawn. After two continues treat as reasoning failure. Background commands/agents still running mean not done.
5. For long slices schedule a fresh verifier against SCOPE. Read only relevant errors/bounded log tails on failure.

## Review path

Every lens gets fresh context, an immutable diff and read access, never the authoring conversation; it reports only. `<review>` = `<root>/.tmp/orchestrated-refactor/<run-id>/review/`. Inputs go in `<review>/in/`, reports in `<review>/out/review-<short-sha>-<lens>-<n>.md` (check absent first; never overwrite a live one). Freeze inputs with `git diff --output="<review>/in/<sha>.diff" <base>...<head>` (delta: `git diff --output="<review>/in/<sha>-delta.diff" <prev-head>..<head>`) and review from `git worktree add --detach "<root>/.tmp/worktrees/<run-id>-review-<short-sha>" <head>`; remove that checkout once its last reviewer ends. Where an `engineering-criteria` skill or copy is available, copy its core file and the files its Packs table selects for the diff into `<review>/in/criteria/`, unchanged, and name that folder in every prompt.

Classes: risky = security, money, migration, infrastructure, dependency or agent-policy (instructions, skills, scripts). Logic-bearing = any other diff that changes a branch, loop, parser, state, cleanup or error path, or a value other code reads. Trivial = non-risky wording, comments, formatting or inert data. Exempt only prose-only docs or typo/comment fixes; record the exemption.

Severity: HIGH = data loss, security exposure or broken primary path in a realistic scenario; MEDIUM = wrong behavior in a realistic secondary scenario; LOW = edge cases, wording, docs, style. A defect that needs a rare coincidence (a narrow race window or an unlikely ordering of events, never input a caller can choose) and fails in the safe direction (it recovers by itself before any deadline it serves, and nothing is lost, exposed, duplicated or wrongly moved, such as money or access) is LOW; an accessibility regression, missing resilience at a network or cloud boundary (class E) or missing required scale work is never rated down this way. Class K is rated by the first of these that fits, never down as rare, since growth is certain: HIGH inside an explicit transaction or while holding a lock that other work waits on (under such a lock it stalls unrelated work; a singleton job's own lease is not one); LOW on a path only an operator runs; HIGH on a path users hit routinely, such as a rule composed into every request or a common list page (it degrades without an error until pages time out); MEDIUM otherwise (an occasional user action, a sweep tick, a batch). A second implementation of a cross-cutting mechanism of the kinds class J lists, an access, money or lifecycle rule decided in more than one place, or a re-implemented shared-package type (class J) is MEDIUM, since the copies drift with the next change to one of them; other duplication is LOW. Every finding needs file:line and a concrete failure scenario.

Reviewer forms (run from the review checkout, in background, in parallel):
- Claude: `claude -p --model opus --tools "Read,Grep,Glob" --strict-mcp-config --permission-mode default --add-dir "<review>/in" < "<prompt-file>" > "<report>"`; the prompt file ends "Put your complete report in your final message; you cannot write files." Only if the CLI is unavailable, use an `Agent` general-purpose reviewer (no isolation) alone, and compare `git rev-parse HEAD` and `git status --porcelain` of the checkouts before/after, since it is read-only only by prompt (writes to ignored paths go undetected).
- Codex (if detected): `codex exec --json -s read-only -m <model> -c model_reasoning_effort=<low|medium|high by size/risk> -c model_auto_compact_token_limit=230000 -c model_auto_compact_token_limit_scope=total -C "<checkout>" --output-last-message "<report>" - < "<prompt-file>" > "<report-stem>.jsonl"`. No `--add-dir` (it grants writes); name the diff path in the prompt.
- Success: exit 0 and a nonempty report that ends in its coverage line (sweep, followed by its leftover hit counts), its coverage line then a verdict (delta), its files-read line and row counts then a verdict (inventory), or a verdict (intent). On failure read the primary error and retry once; a usage-limit/auth error or second failure records the lens unavailable for that head, never clean (a cross-family sweep's usage limit: the out-of-quota rule in the Review path).
  - Size: before launch, split a sweep, delta or inventory lens whose assignment (a delta's is its delta diff) exceeds about 3,000 changed lines or 40 changed files into lenses of the same kind and model by file group, each within that size; a single file over that size gets lenses of its own by hunk range. Each prompt names its files (and hunk ranges) and their count.
  - Incomplete: a sweep, delta or inventory report whose covered count is below its assigned total, or that says it skimmed or skipped files or hunks, is incomplete: not clean and not failed. At once launch a new lens of the same kind and model on its uncovered files, split finer by file group or hunk range, down to a single hunk, until every report covers its whole assignment. An unattended run with no form to launch that lens applies its caller's needs-human signal to the incomplete report instead. A part a lens of its own still cannot cover (one file or hunk) is recorded unavailable for that head, never clean, and goes to the user, who reviews it by hand, waives it with the reason recorded, or blocks the merge (an unattended run applies its caller's needs-human signal); the round waits for that decision.
  - An incomplete lens never satisfies a round, a cap count or the merge gate; the round is done when its lenses together cover the whole assignment (an incomplete lens's covered files count), apart from parts the user decided on.

Prompts:
- Intent: diff, PR intent and claims. Ask for bugs, security issues, missed edge cases, unintended changes, and whether the design holds (claims vs behavior, guards weakened, callers and scope missed). Ends with a verdict.
- Unanchored sweep (no intent): "Report-only line-by-line sweep of <diff> in <checkout>. Judge behavior against the code's own claims. Read every hunk and its dependencies; check A-K; search every removed/renamed identifier. One finding per line: [class] SEVERITY file:line - defect. Scenario: input/state -> wrong outcome. End with files covered/total, naming any file or hunk not read in full, and leftover hit counts." Checklist: A atomicity/races; B comments, docs or messages that describe behavior the code lacks; C parity between things that must match (prod/test hosts, config/defaults, write/read validation); D leftovers of removed identifiers; E exception paths (pass E below verbatim); F null/empty/zero/overflow/culture/missing-config inputs that a real caller, a trust boundary, stored data or configuration can supply (name that source); G disposal and unbounded growth; H vacuous tests, or new non-trivial logic with no check that would fail; I secrets, authz bypass, injection; J code no requirement needs, or a second implementation of a mechanism the repo or design record already has (a lock, idempotency-key format, access enforcement point, notification path, cache eviction or page state and refresh rule) (resilience at network and cloud boundaries and scale and data-access work required by `engineering-criteria` Scale and Data access are not needless); K a query over a table that grows with use whose cost follows the table, not the rows returned (no index behind a filter, join key or paged ordering; OR across correlated subqueries or joined tables; a function or cast on the filtered column; leading-wildcard or payload-text search; a query per row; an unbounded result, or a large id list sent back as parameters; a full selection re-run per chunk; a raised statement-count ceiling without its statement list; any of these inside an explicit transaction or under a held lock other work waits on; never a single lookup by primary or unique key, nor a deliberate whole-table read on an operator-only path, outside such a transaction or lock, that states its reason; name the table, the index, how often the path runs and whether such a transaction or lock is held).
  - **E. Exception paths.** Swallowed failures. A catch/finally throw replacing the original exception. Retries or fallbacks masking an undiagnosed failure or spending their budget on the wrong error. Missing standard resilience; unproven `RemoveAllResilienceHandlers`, disabled SDK retries, `MaxRetries = 0`, custom pipelines or, for transient faults, "next run retries" (`engineering-criteria` Resilience). `RemoveAllResilienceHandlers()` immediately followed by `AddStandardResilienceHandler(o => ...)` that keeps unsafe-method retries off (or, for a keyed client, sets the keyed `Retry.ShouldHandle`; `engineering-criteria` Resilience) is correct for a defaults-inherited options override; flag removal without such a re-add unless its site comment gives a proven reason that `engineering-criteria` allows. Disabling SDK retries for a known non-idempotent, unkeyed operation when the server offers no idempotency key, with a one-line site reason, is correct. The documented shared-helper pattern with cmdlet, curl or github-script built-in retries off and one helper retrying for idempotent calls is also correct.
- Delta: the delta diff, current full diff, checkout and the findings being fixed. Read every changed block and its callers; verify each fix and ask what it broke (cleanup paths, error handling, test isolation, defaults other callers reach, query shape and index coverage of any changed query, the inventory row of any query, entry point or mechanism a fix changed, docs made untrue). Ends with files covered/total of the delta, naming any file or hunk not read in full, then a verdict.
- Inventory lenses (round 1, beside the sweep, when the diff meets their trigger; a trivial diff runs none; record `not run: no trigger` otherwise; a fix set that first brings in a lens's subject adds that lens to its delta, and any delta re-checks the rows its fixes changed): each rebuilds one inventory from the code, never from a worker's rows, which are claims to check, and reports each failing row. They run on the model and family of the round's own sweep, the security lens on the model used for security-sensitive review. Data access, when the diff touches queries, the data model or its configuration, indexes, migrations, raw SQL, bulk writes, transactions, or reach or scope predicates: one row per set query added or changed, per query that composes a changed predicate, and per index or migration change (table and whether it grows, path and how often it runs, transaction or lock held, driving index at file:line or NONE, shape, plan check); a row that fails the query-cost rules is class K, and sound rows that lack a required plan check share one class H MEDIUM finding. Structure, when the diff adds a non-private type, or adds or changes a helper, script, cross-cutting mechanism or a rule in an agent instruction: each new one with the searches run and the nearest existing one, and every implementation or statement of each mechanism or rule the change adds or changes; one the change adds beside an existing one (a shared package's type included), or a copy it changes without the others, is class J at the structural severity. Copies kept on purpose (generated files, a portable or per-harness restatement, a reader with its removal condition, a move the design record marks as in progress) are one implementation; a difference in meaning between them, one edited without the others included, is class J, rated by what a reader of the stale copy would do wrong; implementations the change does not edit are listed, not findings. Security, when the diff adds or changes an entry point or its authentication, authorization or tenant scope: one row per such entry point (principal required, access decision point used, tenant scope, where untrusted input is validated, what is returned or logged); a missing or bypassed control is class I. A cell the code does not settle is written UNRESOLVED; a row whose verdict depends on one is settled from the code or by one more lens before the round's findings are final, and one that still is not goes into the findings at the severity its failure would have, naming the fact that would settle it. Each report ends with files read/total, rows listed, the UNRESOLVED count and a verdict; Success, Size and Incomplete apply as to a sweep. In an orchestrated run they read the integrated diff, never a slice alone: round 1 runs each triggered lens on the full integrated diff.

Rounds:
- A review converges: newly confirmed HIGH and MEDIUM fall round over round to zero inside the cap. One that does not usually has its cause in the design or in a rule specified past its need, which the design lens is there to find (the design trigger's trend rule, below).
- Round 1 before PR, in parallel on full `base...head`: opus intent plus opus unanchored sweep. Risky and logic-bearing diffs add a cross-family unanchored sweep from the family that did not author it: Codex on Claude-authored work if detected. On all-Codex authorship the Claude lenses are already cross-family; record that. Mixed authorship or the other family unavailable: record cross-family unavailable; same-family lenses gate. A cross-family sweep that cannot run because the other family is out of quota (a limit error, or a quota threshold that kept it from launching) is recorded `unavailable (quota)` and the same-family lenses gate, except on a risky PR: there it is owed, the review goes on with its other rounds, and the PR does not merge until that sweep has run on the final head or the user has waived it with the reason recorded. Record `cross-family: owed, quota resets <time>` (or `reset unknown`) in the review table and tell the user. It runs once, when quota allows and the cycle's other rounds have ended, on the head that is final then: one more unanchored sweep, beside the merge-head pass and not in place of it (a cross-family merge-head sweep of that head settles it), counted as that pass is; a HIGH/MEDIUM it confirms gets a fix and a delta. An unattended run on a risky PR records the sweep as owed and does not merge. On a risky or logic-bearing diff with no separate cross-family sweep, add a sonnet second sweep.
- Verify and deduplicate every finding against the code, LOW/nits included; fix as one set or rebut with evidence (cite the type, caller or guard). Weigh likelihood against impact on every finding: a rare, safe-direction defect (severity line above) is rebutted with that evidence, citing file:line of the safe outcome, or given the smallest local fix, never a new mechanism or a refactor of the approach; actual data loss and security exposure still get fixed, and accessibility and required resilience and scale work are never rebutted this way. Any other finding whose cause is in the approach is fixed by refactoring the approach in that set, not by a patch per symptom. Send fixes to the owning worker while its worktree exists, otherwise a new worker/branch from default. A fix brief carries FINDINGS (confirmed, deduplicated findings only, grouped by shared cause; raw reports are named by path, never appended), the worker template's CRITERIA and REUSE lines for what the fixes touch, and a REPORT that restates the inventory row of any query, entry point or mechanism a fix changes. A LOW class F finding on an input that crosses no trust boundary, whose fix would add a branch, option or validation layer, is rebutted on likelihood where its source is unlikely to supply it, naming that source; input that crosses a trust boundary still gets its validation.
- Round 1 fixes that change logic (LOW-only included) get one delta; fixes that are only code comments or human-facing docs do not (in agent instructions and skills, wording is logic). Another delta only after a confirmed HIGH/MEDIUM in the preceding delta. A fix set that replaces an approach gets its delta plus a full unanchored sweep, counted together as one delta. Cap: round 1 plus 2 deltas (3 for integrated diffs over about 2,000 changed lines) per cycle.
- Merge-head pass, outside the cap, at most once per review cycle: if logic changed after round 1, run one orchestrator-family full unanchored sweep of the final head, plus a cross-family sweep, when available (out of quota: the rule above) and the orchestrator family is not already cross-family to every author, on a risky PR or a logic-bearing PR where a cross-family lens raised a confirmed HIGH/MEDIUM. HIGH/MEDIUM from it gets a delta, which counts as extra if the cap is spent.
- No PR merges with an open HIGH or MEDIUM, even past the cap. Deltas past the cap count as extra, the merge-head pass excluded. Two triggers: the design trigger is a HIGH/MEDIUM confirmed by the cap's last planned delta or any later review of cycle 1, or earlier by the trend rule (a delta of cycle 1 that confirms two or more new HIGH/MEDIUM and at least as many as the round or delta before it; a finding raised before and still open is not new), merge-head pass excluded and per area on a Large PR, below; the loop-safety trigger is a HIGH/MEDIUM confirmed by the second extra delta or any later review of a cycle, and ends that cycle. A cycle that ends with nothing open goes on to the merge gates. Every LOW and nit is fixed or explicitly rebutted.
- Redesign cycle, at most once per PR (once per area on a Large PR, below) without the user's approval at a loop-safety stop: when the design trigger fires, before the next fix set, a fresh-context opus design lens reads intent, any design record, the full diff and every round's findings and fixes, and returns `design` (the open findings share a cause in the approach, such as one invariant, data path, ownership or state model; it names the cause, a replacement design (any shared mechanism it needs marked per Phase 1 step 2) and any scope growth that design needs) or `not-design` (independent findings, reviewer churn, contested findings, or a rule or mechanism specified past its need, which it recommends cutting or rebutting); a design lens unavailable after its retry counts as `not-design`. On `not-design`, the current cycle continues (its remaining planned deltas, then extra ones; the trend rule fires once per cycle, and a HIGH/MEDIUM at the cap's last planned delta after it runs the lens again with that diagnosis) and the diagnosis goes to the next fix set and is kept for the stop lens (Loop-safety stop). On `design`, unless it cannot be taken here (next bullet), notify the user (cause, design, scope growth; push notification where available; an unattended run uses only its caller's channel) without waiting, record scope growth in SCOPE/DONE, the handoff and the PR body, dispatch the implementation to workers (unless quota/routing sends it elsewhere), outside a handed `full-review` plan only after Run in flight (Phase 1 step 2) is met, and start the next cycle (cycle 2 after the first redesign) on the new head: full round 1 with authorship and the risk class reassessed, a fresh cap, its own extra deltas and its own merge-head pass. Scope may grow when doing the original intent properly requires it (more files, a changed contract, a dependency or migration); a newly added risky class makes the PR risky from that cycle's round 1, and the merge confirmation rules still apply. A held security or data-exposure fix keeps the cause, design and growth out of the PR and tracked files (only in `.tmp/` review records and the final message); its notice says only that a redesign started.
- A `design` cannot be taken here when the redesign would change the intent or add separable work that belongs on its own branch, when an unattended run (no user present) would need scope growth or depart from an owner-approved specification's design, or when a run executing a handed `full-review` plan would need more than its slices' SCOPE and DONE (never re-planned here). A discovered defect that an unattended run folds in is not this scope growth; a redesign that needs more scope still goes to its caller.
- Large PR (over about 2,000 changed lines): the round 1 of the first cycle in which it is that large records its areas in the review table (file groups, or the design record's lifecycles and shared mechanisms where one exists).
  - Later cycles keep them. File-group areas are re-cut from a design record written after them (Phase 1 step 2, Run in flight) at the next cycle's round 1; a new area overlapping one already redesigned counts as redesigned (its later HIGH/MEDIUMs continue the cycle). A redesign taken before counts toward the bound below.
  - The design trigger, design lens and redesign cycle then apply per area. An area's design trigger is a HIGH/MEDIUM in that area confirmed by a cycle's last planned delta or any later review of that cycle, or earlier by the trend rule applied to that area's counts in that cycle (merge-head pass excluded), in any cycle before that area's redesign. Its lens reads intent, any design record, that area's diff and every round's findings and fixes for it. Each area gets at most one redesign without the user's approval at a loop-safety stop.
  - Areas that trigger on the same review each get their lens, and every `design` among them is implemented in one next cycle.
  - At most three redesign cycles per PR without the user's approval at a loop-safety stop; after the third, a design trigger counts as a loop-safety trigger and the trend rule no longer applies.
  - Every cycle's rounds still review the whole new head; the loop-safety trigger and stop apply to the whole PR.
- Loop-safety stop: when the loop-safety trigger ends any cycle, or a `design` cannot be taken here, stop; nothing further is implemented until the user decides. A review that fires both the design trigger and the loop-safety trigger is a loop-safety stop. Before reporting a loop-safety trigger, run one stop lens for the whole PR, whatever its size or areas: the design lens in fresh context, with its inputs above plus every earlier diagnosis and redesign. Its verdict is the report's recommendation: `design` (cause, replacement design, scope growth), `not-design` (what keeps the findings coming and what to cut or rebut) or, when it fails after its retry, `unavailable`, never `not-design` by default. The user's approval of a `design` at this stop, whether the stop lens returned it or it could not be taken here (its reserved change or scope growth), starts the next cycle as above, within the bounds above or past them; none is taken without that approval. An approved `design` keeps the limits on what can be taken here: one that needs more than a handed `full-review` plan's SCOPE and DONE is approved as a `full-review` re-run, never growth in place, since held weaknesses may sit near the grown scope, and separable work still goes on its own branch. Report the open findings, every cycle's fix history and the stop lens's verdict, or the `design` that could not be taken here, to the user; merge waits for their decision (an unattended run applies its caller's needs-human signal instead, with it through its caller's channel; a held security or data-exposure fix, attended or not, keeps it out of the PR and tracked files, in `.tmp/` review records and the final message).
- Record every round (cycle, head, lenses/models with each split lens's file group and coverage, findings, dispositions, unavailable lenses, fixes no reviewer read) in the PR body's review table and the tracked handoff, with a convergence line under the table (newly confirmed HIGH and MEDIUM per round, in order; per area on a Large PR).

## Integrate and merge

Only the orchestrator opens and merges PRs. For each PR (one per increment, Ship in increments below), integrate its slice branches onto one branch, run the full affected checks locally, and run Review path round 1 on the integrated diff (slice checks never substitute). Then `git push -u origin <branch>` and open that PR (via `gh` if detected) stating what, why, validation and the review table; later rounds follow on the PR. Before merge, audit the full `base...head`: intended scope only, no secrets or stray artifacts (`.tmp/`, test output, logs), no unintended dependency, lockfile, migration, CI workflow or infrastructure change; record the audit in the PR. Merge only with local checks passing, required CI green, review done/exempt with no open HIGH/MEDIUM, and the audit clean. When the default branch gained commits touching files the PR changes, first merge it into the branch, rerun affected checks and review a resolution that changes logic. Merge by squash. Never push to the default branch directly or force-push shared branches. Confirm with the user before any merge that deploys, publishes, migrates data or changes credentials. If Graphify was detected and the change is material, offer a graph refresh as its own commit.

Configuration gate: supported configurations are the interchangeable configurations the repo declares (its instructions, settings switches or provider lists, never guessed: providers of one dependency such as a database or message broker, cache or storage backends, OS targets, feature-flag states that switch code paths, a rollout flag's off and on states included). A change to code whose behavior can differ between them (data access and query translation, locking, collation or case rules, serialization, provider-specific SQL, platform conditionals) runs the narrowest check that exercises it on every supported configuration, not only the default: each axis's values one at a time from a baseline that reaches the changed code (a flag stays in the state that runs it), combinations only where the repo declares them. At each integration of such a slice the orchestrator runs those checks on every configuration before the next slice builds on it, not only before the PR, and records each configuration's command, host and result in the handoff and the PR. A tier CI runs only on manual dispatch records the local or remote run that covered it; "not run" is never reported as passing.

Gate duration: record each test tier's duration with its result at every integration (tier, configuration, tests run, duration, machine). Compare like with like, the same configuration on the same machine: before the first integration on a machine, record the duration of the run's starting default-branch commit for each tier and configuration there as its baseline. A tier fails the gate when, against its baseline or against its last recorded duration on this run, it takes over 1.5 times as long and at least two minutes longer, without a matching rise in tests run: before the next slice builds on it, compare per-test duration by run position against the default branch and, where the tier uses a database, read its slow-statement log. Duration that rises with run position over a shared database most often comes from a statement whose cost follows a growing table; fix what the log shows at its cause. A rise diagnosed as something other than a defect (a new slow test, with its reason) is recorded in the handoff with the new baseline; a query-cost defect is fixed, never accepted. Machine load is a hypothesis to prove (a rerun on an idle machine), never the default explanation; a longer timeout, more parallelism or a per-test database reset is not a fix.

Ship in increments: work larger than one reviewable PR (about 2,000 changed lines) ships as several PRs in dependency order, the mechanism slices (slice 0 and any split of it) first, each merged to default behind the feature's rollout flag (the repo's existing config or flag provider, never a new one without approval, and a removal plan) or, for a refactor, each leaving default working; never one long-lived branch. Each PR's integrated diff gets its own Review path; later slices branch from default after the PRs they depend on merge. A handed `full-review` plan keeps its PR grouping; a grouped PR over about 2,000 changed lines takes the larger cap (Review path) and the Large PR rule.

After each verified merge, preserve useful worker decisions in the tracked handoff. Stop the dev servers, watchers, test hosts, build servers and background shells that PR's slices and reviews started before removing those slices' clean worktrees, branches and state and that PR's review checkouts, so nothing holds a file handle; other slices, and entries kept for the user's decision, stay. At run end remove run scratch and confirm no run worktrees, branches or state remain except those kept for the user's decision, listed in the handoff. Leave every entry outside this run's slice table and review checkouts alone.

## Session handoff

Before ending, update active count, queue, slices, paths, decisions, checks, Environment table and exact next action. List every deliberately kept worktree/state/review input. Never unlock, remove or reuse another session's entries. A later session resumes from the tracked handoff alone; replacement workers use their own handoff and last commit.

## Token discipline

- Prefer a few complete slices to tiny spawns.
- Scope and retrieve better instead of raising tier/effort for long prompts.
- Read completion reports and diffs, never full transcripts or JSONL logs.
